description: We are Batangas State University students from Batangas City, Philippines, driven by curiosity about space and a desire to learn through real-world challenges. Through this hackathon, we aim to turn our technology skills into a practical space mission application, while growing as developers, designers, and problem-solvers.
summary:
Welcome to MOONWARD, GitCantCommit’s lunar mission-planning game for NASA’s Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. You play the mission planner. A payload needs sunlight, a view of Earth, or both, and you must decide where and when to operate on the Moon.

Tools like JPL Horizons, LROC QuickMap, and NASA Moon Trek are hard for non-specialists to use. Moonward turns their data into a hands-on game. Pin two landing options on a Moon map, drag the mission clock, and read separate tracks for sunlight and Earth visibility. Open a horizon view to see the Sun, Earth, and local terrain at any moment, or step into a cozy lunar diorama to look along the bearing of a ridge. Then Mission Control sends a dispatch: “The landing date slipped. Can we still do the job?” Keep the site, move the site, or hold the operation, and file a short decision brief explaining why.

Along the way you learn why continuous sunlight matters more than total sunlight, how terrain can block the Sun while it is still above the horizon, and why Earth visibility is not the same as a working radio link.

Landing-site selection is one of the hardest parts of lunar exploration, especially near the poles, where water ice raises the stakes. Moonward lets players practice rapid evaluation of landing sites and see themselves as explorers of the Moon.
details:
Moonward: A Lunar Landing-Site and Mission-Timing Planning Game

Moonward is an interactive, browser-based lunar mission-planning game developed by Team GitCantCommit for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It makes complex lunar exploration concepts more accessible by turning scientific data into a hands-on, educational game. Planning a mission to the Moon means weighing sunlight availability, Earth visibility, terrain, and scientific objectives. Platforms such as LROC QuickMap, NASA Moon Trek, and JPL Horizons provide valuable information, but non-specialists often find them hard to interpret. Moonward lets players experience the decision-making process of a lunar mission instead. Players act as the mission planner. A payload needs a stretch of sunlight, a view of Earth, or both, and the player must recommend where and when to operate. Players pin two plans on a Moon map, each combining a site, a UTC start time, and a task duration. They can compare two sites at the same time, or two start times at the same site, using a scrubbable mission clock with separate tracks for sunlight and Earth visibility. The launch scope includes a historical site, Tranquility Base, and a candidate study point near the lunar south pole. Both are assessed in a hypothetical future exploration-era window whose dates are chosen from the generated data. The featured mission, Change of Plans, delivers a dispatch from Mission Control: “The landing date slipped. Can we still do the job?” The player decides whether to keep the site, move the site, or hold the operation. Along the way, players discover how a small change in location or timing can make or break a mission.

Moonward is built with Godot 4, GDScript, and the Compatibility renderer, and is designed first for a judge using a PC browser, with direct access and no account. It uses precomputed science data. NASA JPL Horizons supplies time-stamped Sun and Earth directions for an observer at each selected lunar coordinate. The Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) aboard NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, together with NASA Goddard polar terrain products, supplies the elevation data used to build the local terrain and skyline. Players can drag the task bracket along the timeline, see whether the whole task fits inside continuous full sunlight, and click a break in the timeline to open a compass-aligned horizon view of the Sun, Earth, and terrain at that moment. They can also step into a cozy HD-2D lunar diorama with a four-direction pixel astronaut, viewed in third person for scale or first person to look along the bearing of a ridge. Finally, they file a recommendation in a one-screen Mission Log that records the chosen plan, the alternative, the decisive interval, the remaining margin, and any unresolved questions. Scientific accuracy is a release criterion for every result. Sunlight is evaluated against the airless local skyline, so “full sunlight ends” and “the Sun disappears” are shown as different events. Each verdict reads Meets, Misses, or Unknown, and every scored mission carries its coordinates, UTC range, observer height, source products, and limitations. The team also considered data reliability, terrain coverage, accessibility, keyboard controls, and educational value, so that the game stays engaging while encouraging players to understand the reasoning behind their decisions.

The creativity of Moonward lies in combining real lunar data with a short, replayable decision game. Rather than presenting astronomical information only through charts and technical tools, it lets players apply scientific observations to make decisions that change their mission’s outcome. Players learn that continuous time matters more than total time, because two separate periods of sunlight cannot cover a task that needs one uninterrupted observation. They learn that terrain can block the Sun while it is still above the level horizon. They also learn the limits of a result: sunlight is evidence for solar-power planning but not proof of battery endurance, and Earth visibility is a geometric communication opportunity, not a confirmed radio link. A justified hold counts as a successful planning decision, and every case has an ending, so missing evidence never traps the player in a retry loop. The game highlights how hard landing-site selection is, especially in polar regions where uneven terrain, changing illumination, and the possible presence of water ice raise the stakes. Moonward’s intended impact is to make lunar science more understandable and engaging for students, space enthusiasts, and the general public, and to show how game development can support science education. By letting players practice rapid evaluation of landing-site options, it aims to inspire interest in astronomy, space technology, and future lunar missions, and to show why careful planning matters in space exploration.
